source.title: Why We Build Local Large Language Models: An Observational Analysis from 35 Japanese and Multilingual LLMs
source.authors: Koshiro Saito; Sakae Mizuki; Masanari Ohi; Taishi Nakamura; Taihei Shiotani; Koki Maeda; Youmi Ma; Kakeru Hattori; Kazuki Fujii; Takumi Okamoto; Shigeki Ishida; Hiroya Takamura; Rio Yokota; Naoaki Okazaki

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or document mismatch. Some table and figure content is flattened, but the text reports the correlations recorded below.
record.tranche_reason: The study examines associations between computational budgets and benchmark-derived ability scores using observational correlations and PCA, rather than measuring held-out loss or running the original scaling-law experiments.
record.gate_note: The study reports correlations between language-specific computational budgets and PCA or factor-analysis scores derived from benchmark performance. It does not report held-out cross-entropy loss, fit loss power laws, test extrapolation from small runs, or search for compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Per-benchmark scores are evaluated, but results not tied to the scaling or fit-dependence analyses are not recorded as rows here.
record.test_reason: The study correlates log compute budget (parameters × tokens, total or per language) across 35 existing base LLMs with PCA ability scores from 19 benchmarks. This is an observational test of whether downstream performance scales with compute (V6). It does not measure loss, fit loss power laws, test extrapolation, search for an optimal allocation, or compare fitting choices for loss laws.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. PC1 (general ability) scales with English (or total) compute, and PC2 (Japanese knowledge QA and English-to-Japanese translation) scales with Japanese compute but not English or total compute. Tasks like academic subjects, math and code transfer across languages, so they do not need Japanese data. The paraphrase should add that the authors found no scaling law for PC3.
record.recipe_differences: Observational analysis of benchmark scores across existing models, using PCA or factor analysis and correlations with language-specific parameter-count-times-token budgets; it does not measure held-out loss or fit the original loss scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The alternative maximum-likelihood factor analysis with Promax rotation changes the interpretation of some factors: its first factor appears English-specific rather than general, while its fourth factor is treated as a residual. Excluding continually pretrained models yields similar reported budget–ability correlations.
record.problems: The evidence is observational across heterogeneous models and does not establish causal effects. Computational budgets depend partly on estimated language-token shares. The study uses benchmark-derived factor scores rather than held-out loss and reports correlations rather than out-of-sample prediction tests.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed per-model benchmark scores and other task-level results are not included because the recorded scaling analyses report aggregate budget–factor associations; the study provides those benchmark results in its evaluation figures and the referenced Zenodo dataset.

untested.parts: Held-out loss versus N, D or C; no loss is measured.
No fits on small runs and no extrapolation to larger runs.
No compute-optimal allocation of parameters versus tokens.
No comparison of depth or width at a fixed parameter count.
No other modalities or regimes. Continual pretraining is included but is not analysed as a separate scaling law.
Predictive validity: no held-out-model prediction and no fitted slope uncertainty. No relation to pretraining loss. Per-benchmark scaling is not analysed.
No fitted exponents and no comparison of fitting methods for loss or compute laws.

missing.what: Factor 1 (English ability) versus English budget and Factor 3 (Japanese ability) versus Japanese budget under Promax factor analysis; no values are stated in the text
The authors state that no scaling law was identified for PC3 (arithmetic reasoning and code ability); this negative result is not recorded as a row
Qualitative observation that larger models score higher within each model group

record.verdict_notes: The scaling analysis is observational across heterogeneous published models. Language token counts are often estimated by fixed ratios, and the models with unknown counts are excluded (n = 27 or 25). The rows are correlations of PCA scores, not fitted power laws of benchmark accuracy. The V7 label in the record is removed because the factor-rotation robustness check concerns PCA interpretation, not fitting of scaling laws.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameter count, tokens, or compute; power-law form and several-orders-of-magnitude range.
No predictions from small-run loss-law fits are compared with larger runs.
No fixed-compute optimization or estimated compute-optimal parameter/token split.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
The study concerns text pretraining and does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer regimes.
The study reports observational associations between compute budgets and benchmark-derived ability scores, but does not validate predictions on held-out models or test relations to pretraining loss.
It checks sensitivity to factor-analysis choices, but does not compare fitted loss-law exponents, compute-optimal splits, or departures of loss curves from a power law.

relationships.condition: General ability (PC1) versus English or total budget, and Japanese ability (PC2) versus Japanese budget; full set and from-scratch subset
relationships.reason: Strong log-linear correlations: ρ = 0.916, 0.938 and 0.923 for PC1; ρ = 0.779 for PC2 in both the full and from-scratch sets (r1, r2, r5, r6, r7). These are observational associations only.
relationships.display_finding: General ability has log-linear budget correlations of 0.916, 0.938 and 0.923, while Japanese ability correlates at 0.779 in both the full and from-scratch sets.

relationships.condition: Language-specific ability (PC2) against total or English compute; arithmetic and code ability (PC3)
relationships.reason: PC2 barely correlates with total budget (0.186) or English budget (0.164) (r3, r4), so total scale does not predict local-knowledge or translation ability. The text also states no scaling law was identified for PC3; no row records this.
relationships.display_finding: Language-specific ability correlated only 0.186 with total compute and 0.164 with English compute, while no scaling law was identified for arithmetic and code ability.
